reference.source: ESC/ERS Guidelines for Pulmonary Hypertension / Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: Defined by breathlessness (platypnoea) and arterial desaturation (orthodeoxia) that appear or worsen on sitting or standing upright and improve on lying flat
Reflects a posture-dependent right-to-left shunt, most often intracardiac through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect, but sometimes intrapulmonary
Intracardiac cases frequently require an anatomical or functional distortion, such as an enlarged or unfolded aorta, that redirects venous flow across the septum when upright
Intrapulmonary causes include hepatopulmonary syndrome and pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, especially with basal-predominant shunting
Contrast (bubble) echocardiography, ideally with postural manoeuvres, is central to localising the shunt as intracardiac or intrapulmonary
Oxygen supplementation often only partially corrects the hypoxaemia because of true shunt physiology
Percutaneous or surgical closure of an intracardiac defect can be curative, whereas intrapulmonary causes are managed according to their underlying disease
reference.pathophysiology: Platypnoea-orthodeoxia syndrome arises from a right-to-left shunt whose magnitude increases in the upright posture. In the intracardiac form there is an interatrial communication such as a patent foramen ovale, but the shunt only becomes haemodynamically significant when an additional anatomical or functional factor, for example an elongated or dilated aortic root, right pneumonectomy, or pericardial change, alters the geometry of the atria so that inferior vena caval flow is preferentially directed across the septum on standing. In the intrapulmonary form, dilated or abnormal vessels at the lung bases, as seen in hepatopulmonary syndrome or arteriovenous malformations, receive more perfusion when upright, increasing the fraction of venous blood bypassing gas exchange. In both mechanisms, standing augments the shunt and produces the characteristic positional hypoxaemia and breathlessness.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (e.g. hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia)
Patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect without other cause
Chronic parenchymal lung disease with basal shunting
Autonomic or orthostatic disorders mimicking positional symptoms
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gases measured both supine and upright to document orthodeoxia
Contrast (agitated saline) echocardiography with postural manoeuvres to localise the shunt
Transoesophageal echocardiography to define interatrial anatomy
CT or MR imaging to identify aortic, mediastinal, or pulmonary vascular abnormalities
Technetium macroaggregated albumin scan to quantify an intrapulmonary shunt
Assessment for liver disease when hepatopulmonary syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Severe positional hypoxaemia limiting the patient to a recumbent posture
Hypoxaemia poorly responsive to supplemental oxygen, indicating true shunt
Paradoxical embolic events such as stroke through an intracardiac shunt
Rapidly progressive desaturation suggesting worsening shunt fraction
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; closure of a responsible intracardiac defect is frequently curative with immediate resolution of the positional hypoxaemia. Intrapulmonary causes carry the prognosis of the underlying pulmonary or hepatic disease.
pitfalls: Measuring oxygenation only supine and thereby missing orthodeoxia
Assuming an incidental patent foramen ovale is sufficient without seeking the anatomical factor that makes it shunt
Failing to distinguish intracardiac from intrapulmonary shunting before intervention
Attributing positional breathlessness to deconditioning or anxiety
Overlooking hepatopulmonary syndrome as an intrapulmonary cause
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
